questions.problem: Suppose $|\,p\,|=10\sqrt{2}$ and the angle between vectors $p$ and $q$ is $\theta ={45}^{∘}.$ Find the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p & =|\,p\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =10\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({45}^{∘}) \\  & =10\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components
questions.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,d\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}+{d}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 2+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{c}\,d & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,c\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{c}_{x}^{2}+{c}_{y}^{2}+{c}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{25}} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c-{\text{comp}}_{c}\,d & =\frac{11}{3}-\frac{11}{5} \\  & =11(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =11(\frac{5}{15}-\frac{3}{15}) \\  & =\frac{22}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components
questions.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,d\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}+{d}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 1+0\cdot (-2)}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{c}\,d & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,c\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{c}_{x}^{2}+{c}_{y}^{2}+{c}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{25}} \\  & =\frac{5}{5} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c-{\text{comp}}_{c}\,d & =\frac{5}{3}-1 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $p=⟨\sqrt{2},1,-1⟩$ and $q=⟨\sqrt{8},-\sqrt{3},1⟩.$ Find the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,q\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}+{q}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{8}+1\cdot (-\sqrt{3})+(-1)\cdot 1}{\sqrt{(\sqrt{8})^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3-\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{3-\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Projecting a Vector Onto a Perpendicular Vector
questions.problem: Let $p=⟨2,0,3⟩$ and $q=⟨3,0,x⟩.$ Given that the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q$ is zero, find the value of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $p$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $q$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
p⊥q\,⟹\,p\cdot q=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =2\cdot 3+0\cdot 0+3\cdot x \\  & =3x+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =0 \\ 3x+6 & =0 \\ 3x & =-6 \\ x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ x \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Given that the scalar projection of $a$ onto $b$ is $0,$ find the value of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =0\cdot (-2)+(-2)\cdot x+1\cdot 2 \\  & =2-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 2-2x & =0 \\ 2x & =2 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

$$
